title: Equivalence of the global retrieval phase of the inverse model on the Nishimori line and the spin-glass phase of the direct model
content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks, the inverse model (student) learns a teacher pattern from examples generated by a teacher network. The direct model is a dense Hopfield network with \(M\) random memorized patterns. On the Nishimori line, where the student has the same interaction order \(p\) and inverse temperature \(\beta\) as the teacher (\(p=p^*\), \(\beta=\beta^*\)), the global retrieval phase (\(gR\)) of the inverse model—where the student can retrieve the teacher pattern from any initial condition—coincides with the spin-glass phase of the direct model—where the network freezes in random states with zero magnetization \(m\) (overlap with any stored memory) and positive spin-glass order parameter \(q\) (overlap between two replicas). This refines the quiet planting bound, which states that the learning phase of the inverse model extends at least as far as the spin-glass phase of the direct model, by showing that the learning phase extends exactly as far.

title: Extensive noise tolerance with mismatched interaction orders in the large-noise scaling
content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks with mismatched interaction orders, a student network with interaction order \(p \geq 3\) can learn a teacher pattern from a teacher with interaction order \(p^*=2\) even when the teacher's inverse temperature \(\beta^*\) scales as \(\mathcal{O}(N^{2/p-1})\) (i.e., the teacher noise is extensive), provided the student is given \(M \sim \mathcal{O}(N^{p-1})\) examples, where \(N\) is the number of components per pattern. For \(p=4\), this yields a noise tolerance of \(\mathcal{O}(N^{1/2})\), meaning the teacher's inverse temperature can be as low as \(\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/2})\). The student's learning performance is optimal when the effective inverse temperature \(\lambda = \frac{[\beta^*]^{p/2}}{(p/2)!} N^{p/2-1}\) equals the student's inverse temperature \(\beta\).

title: Exact formula for adversarial robustness at zero temperature for mismatched interaction orders
content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks with teacher interaction order \(p^*=2\), student interaction order \(p \geq 3\) (even), and zero student temperature (\(\beta = \infty\)), the student pattern is initialized as a mixture of the teacher pattern and a single noisy example \(\sigma^a\): a fraction \(\varepsilon\) of its entries are taken from \(\sigma^a\) and the rest from the teacher pattern. The largest fraction \(\varepsilon^*\) for which the student still converges to the teacher pattern (rather than to the example) is \(\varepsilon^* = \frac{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}}{[\eta\alpha]^{1/(p-1)}+1}\), where \(\alpha = \frac{M(p/2+1)!}{N^{p/2}}\) is the finite-noise load (with \(M\) the number of examples and \(N\) the pattern dimension), and \(\eta\) is a parameter depending on the teacher's inverse temperature \(\beta^*\) and \(p\) (for \(p=4\), \(\eta = \frac{2[\beta^*]^2}{(1-2\beta^*)^2}\)). This formula shows that adversarial robustness increases monotonically with the dataset size \(\alpha\).

title: Clarification of adversarial robustness dependence on learning regime in dense Hopfield networks
content: In dense Hopfield networks, adversarial robustness depends on the learning regime. The example Retrieval phase (\(eR\)), also called the prototype phase, is inherently robust because retrieving an example is equivalent to recovering the teacher pattern (the signal). In contrast, the global Retrieval phase (\(gR\)), also called the feature phase, can be vulnerable when it overlaps with the inaccurate \(eR\) phase, where the student pattern has finite overlap with a noisy example but zero overlap with the teacher pattern. Increasing the dataset size \(\alpha\) (the number of examples per pattern dimension) stabilizes the \(gR\) phase and increases robustness, which explains why larger neural networks are often more adversarially robust.

title: Precise location of the paramagnetic-to-spin-glass transition in the direct model via the inverse model on the Nishimori line
content: In the teacher-student setting for dense Hopfield networks on the Nishimori line (where the student has the same interaction order \(p\) and inverse temperature \(\beta\) as the teacher: \(p=p^*\), \(\beta=\beta^*\)), the global retrieval (\(gR\)) phase transition of the inverse model coincides with the exact paramagnetic-to-spin-glass (\(P\)-\(SG\)) phase transition of the direct model (a dense Hopfield network with \(M\) random patterns) for any \(p\), provided the temperature \(T = 1/\beta\) is above the critical temperature \(T_{\text{crit}}\) of the direct model with a single pattern. This equivalence allows the \(P\)-\(SG\) transition to be located precisely using the replica-symmetric (RS) solution of the inverse model, which avoids the numerical instability that arises in one-step replica symmetry breaking (1RSB) calculations for the direct model at large \(p\).

title: Independence of learning performance from number of hidden units for uncorrelated teacher patterns in RBMs
content: In the teacher-student setting for restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) with binary visible and hidden units, where the teacher has \(P^*\) hidden units with uncorrelated patterns (covariance matrix \(\mathcal{Q} = \mathbf{I}\)) and the student has \(P\) hidden units, the student's learning performance, measured by the magnetization \(m\) (the expected overlap between a teacher pattern and a student pattern), is independent of \(P\) and \(P^*\) for any finite \(P, P^*\). The critical data load \(\alpha_{\text{crit}} = M/N\) (where \(M\) is the number of training examples and \(N\) the number of visible units) above which learning becomes possible is \(\alpha_{\text{crit}} = 1/[\beta^*\beta]^2\), which also does not depend on \(P\) or \(P^*\). This validates the conjecture of Barra et al. (2017) and generalizes the results of Hou et al. (2019) from \(P=P^*=2\) to arbitrary finite \(P\) and \(P^*\).

title: Factorization and low-dimensional learning in overparameterized RBMs under the PSB ansatz
content: In the teacher-student setting for restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) with uncorrelated teacher patterns (covariance \(\mathcal{Q} = \mathbf{I}\)), under the permutation symmetry breaking (PSB) ansatz, an RBM with \(P\) hidden units factorizes into \(P\) independent RBMs with one hidden unit each. When the student has more hidden units than the teacher (\(P > P^*\)), exactly \(P^*\) student patterns learn the teacher patterns one-to-one, with magnetization \(m\) (overlap with teacher pattern) and spin-glass overlap \(q\) (overlap between two independent student replicas) satisfying \(m = q\). The remaining \(P - P^*\) student patterns freeze in spin-glass states with zero magnetization and a different spin-glass overlap \(g\). This demonstrates an implicitly low-dimensional learning strategy, where only a subset of hidden units are used to learn the data.
